strengths: Clear problem motivation with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1) that token order significantly affects AR-based classification outcomes

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple baseline families, OOD benchmarks, and real-world distribution shifts with thorough ablations (likelihood strategies, tokenizers, per-token analysis)

Strong empirical results: outperforms diffusion classifiers, achieves competitive performance with DINOv2, and demonstrates significant efficiency gains (25× faster), representing first GC approach competitive with state-of-the-art SSL
Excellent analysis and visualization of order effects through per-token likelihood heatmaps and prefix length studies, providing intuitive understanding of why marginalization improves performance
Fair experimental design with consistent model architectures, resolutions, and sizes across baselines; proper handling of methods without public checkpoints through careful re-implementation
Technically sound use of Jensen's inequality for deriving order-unconditional likelihood lower bound with reasonable hypothesis for why it outperforms direct likelihood estimation
Strong reproducibility: detailed appendices with hyperparameters, model settings, and promise of code/model release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core contribution is applying existing RandAR model with straightforward ensemble averaging over permutations—no new architecture, objective, or tokenization scheme introduced

Incomplete theoretical understanding of why order marginalization improves classification; lacks rigorous analysis of order complementarity, conditions enabling improvement, and what different orders capture
Heavy dependence on RandAR's specific architecture with position encodings; limited exploration of generalization to other any-order AR models or whether insights are broadly applicable

Computational cost scaling with number of classes not adequately addressed: K×M forward passes (K orders, M classes) becomes prohibitive for large-class problems; efficiency advantage overstated given this linear scaling

Order selection (K=20) appears arbitrary, matching diffusion timesteps without principled justification; insufficient analysis of benefit saturation or optimal K selection across computational budgets
Competitive but not dominant over DINOv2: RandAR-XL trails by 1.4% on IN-Val (81.3% vs 82.7%) and significantly on IN-A (23.3% vs 36.3%), somewhat weakening 'competitive performance' claims

Tokenizer sensitivity: different VQ-VAE tokenizers show material performance differences; latent noise augmentation required for LlamaGen but not MaskGIT suggests potential brittleness; WILDS experiments use different tokenizer than main experiments (inconsistency)
Evaluation limited to 256×256 resolution and image classification; no investigation of higher resolutions, other visual domains, or transfer learning scenarios; timing breakdown not provided
Limited exploration of whether orders capture complementary information; no investigation of structured vs. random order sampling strategies or connection between order structure and performance
Class token interaction with position instructions and permutations insufficiently explained; RandAR training from scratch without exploration of transfer learning or pretrained variants

strengths: Clear identification and visual demonstration of token order bias as a limitation of fixed-order AR models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet variants, distribution shifts, WILDS) with thorough ablations and fair baseline comparisons
Strong empirical results showing improvements over diffusion classifiers and competitiveness with DINOv2 on out-of-distribution benchmarks
Effective interpretability analysis via per-token discriminative log-likelihoods that explains how order marginalization captures broader class information
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, code/models promised, multiple baselines reimplemented from scratch
Impressive efficiency gains (25× faster than diffusion classifiers) while maintaining competitive accuracy
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward application of existing RandAR model with Jensen's inequality-based ensemble averaging over random orders; minimal methodological or theoretical contribution
Unclear conceptual advantage over prior ensemble methods (e.g., A-VARC): paper does not rigorously explain why order marginalization is fundamentally superior to other averaging strategies

Significant practical limitations inadequately addressed: (1) requires K=20 forward passes; (2) cannot evaluate on full 1000-class ImageNet (only 2K subsets due to computational cost); (3) still ~1000× slower than discriminative models despite 25× speedup vs diffusion

Shallow understanding of mechanism: why different token orders provide complementary information is not rigorously analyzed beyond intuition; connection to diffusion's coarse-to-fine generation remains speculative
High sensitivity to tokenization choices: results depend on VQ-VAE (MaskGIT vs LlamaGen); requires ad-hoc latent noise augmentation for LlamaGen; suggests brittle approach

Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or variance analysis across random seeds despite stochastic order sampling; claims based on 2K subset evaluations may not reflect full-dataset significance

Incomplete baseline fairness: DINOv2 pretrained on ImageNet-21K while RandAR uses only ImageNet-1K; unclear if poor performance of some AR baselines reflects training differences vs fundamental limitations
Limited analysis of key design choices: why K=20? How does K scale with number of classes? Diminishing returns visible in Figure 5 but not exploited
Restricted scope: vision-only, single-label classification; generalization to other tasks unclear; tied to RandAR architecture limiting broader applicability

strengths: Clear and well-motivated insight about token order limitations in AR-based classifiers, effectively illustrated with compelling examples (Figure 1) and validated through detailed per-token analysis (Figures 3-5)
Solid technical approach using Jensen's inequality to bound order-unconditional likelihood with sound empirical justification via thorough ablations

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet, ImageNet-R/S/A/C, WILDS) with fair comparison setup ensuring same architectures, model sizes, and resolutions across all baselines

Strong empirical results demonstrating consistent improvements over diffusion classifiers and competitive performance with state-of-the-art self-supervised method DINOv2, particularly on OOD benchmarks (3/5 superior, 1/5 tied)
Significant practical efficiency gains (25× speedup over DiT) with single forward pass per order, making generative classification more practical for deployment

Thorough experimental rigor including diverse baselines (discriminative, diffusion, joint models, AR variants), detailed ablations on tokenizers/loss weighting/likelihood strategies, and evaluation on real-world distribution shifts
Insightful analysis revealing that middle-prefix tokens (50-80) are most discriminative and visualizations effectively demonstrating why order marginalization captures more comprehensive signals
High reproducibility: detailed model settings, official implementation adherence, promised code release, and standalone reproduction of baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of Jensen's inequality to bound likelihood and average over random orders, primarily combining existing RandAR architecture with a simple averaging scheme rather than introducing fundamentally new methods

Theoretical justification for why lower bound outperforms direct likelihood for classification is somewhat hand-wavy; the claim that 'RandAR was trained directly on Equation 5' needs deeper analysis of how training objective relates to evaluation objective for classification

Comparison with DINOv2 not entirely conclusive: RandAR-XL trails by 1.4% on in-domain accuracy (0.813 vs 0.827), with mixed OOD performance (3/5 superior, 1/5 tied, 1/5 inferior); the 'competitive performance' claim is somewhat overstated

Computational cost remains prohibitively high for practical large-scale deployment: requires K=20 forward passes per class (20,000 evaluations for 1000-class problems), necessitating 2K subsets for WILDS evaluation; WILDS results being computed on subsets weakens their significance

Key design choices lack principled justification: K=20 appears arbitrary with no investigation of K>20 or diminishing returns; uniform random sampling is simplistic with no exploration of intelligent ordering (e.g., coarse-to-fine) or adaptive strategies

Limited failure mode analysis: Section 6.3 identifies failure types but doesn't demonstrate specific cases where single-order fails while order-marginalized succeeds, missing opportunity to directly validate the core hypothesis
Incomplete comparisons: A-VARC's likelihood smoothing method not detailed, SiT's underperformance versus DiT not investigated despite acknowledged, some concurrent AR work potentially missing

Generalization concerns: evaluation concentrated on ImageNet and variants with only one additional downstream benchmark (WILDS); no evaluation on non-natural image domains despite WILDS containing such data

Missing analyses: no investigation of variance across random permutations, no analysis of logit correlations to understand captured signals, center-object bias in Figure 4 persists despite order marginalization but not discussed

Presentation: connection between DMs' implicit coarse-to-fine ordering and why AR models need explicit order marginalization could be clearer; π notation could be introduced more intuitively; Figure 1 shows only 2 examples despite being core motivation

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet variants, WILDS distribution shifts, ObjectNet, COCO) with consistent experimental protocols demonstrating clear improvements over diffusion classifiers and competitive performance with DINOv2

Clear and well-motivated insight identifying token order as an important inductive bias in AR classifiers, with compelling visualizations (Figure 1) and thorough interpretability analysis (per-token likelihoods, per-token accuracy) explaining how order marginalization works
Significant efficiency gains: 25× faster than DiT while maintaining superior accuracy across most benchmarks, addressing a practical limitation of generative classifiers

Particularly strong out-of-distribution robustness, outperforming both diffusion-based and discriminative baselines on multiple OOD sets, plus superior performance on WILDS distribution shift benchmarks

Thorough ablations and analysis including VQ-VAE tokenizer comparison with noise robustness analysis, likelihood estimation strategy validation, generalization beyond RandAR, and proper formalization of connection to masked diffusion
First comparative study of generative classifiers against state-of-the-art self-supervised methods (DINOv2), providing valuable perspective on generative vs discriminative approaches

Technical soundness with proper mathematical derivations, fair comparisons using consistent architectures/resolutions/token counts, and reproducibility through promised code release and detailed implementation specifications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is a straightforward application of order ensembling to an existing model (RandAR), lacking novel algorithmic insights or theoretical advances beyond identifying that averaging over orders helps

Strong architectural dependency: method requires RandAR, one of few any-order AR models; generalization demonstrated only with RAR-B; severely restricts applicability and impact, requiring practitioners to wait for compatible models

Incomplete theoretical understanding of why order marginalization helps beyond ensemble averaging—lacks principled analysis of whether benefits stem from coverage, voting mechanisms, or deeper structural properties of random image token orders

Notable performance gap with DINOv2: 1.4% lower on ImageNet-Val (81.3% vs 82.7%), significantly lower on IN-A (23.3% vs 36.3%), and DINOv2 trained on more data (ImageNet-21K+1K vs 1K only), complicating fair comparison

Unjustified choice of likelihood lower bound (Eq. 5) over direct likelihood estimate: explanation that 'RandAR was trained on Eq. 5' is post-hoc rationalization; raises questions about whether models optimize for intended objectives versus observed training procedure

Significant tokenization dependency: performance varies with VQ-VAE choice (1-2% differences), latent noise augmentation required only for LlamaGen, and unclear why design is not robust across tokenizers; introduces additional moving parts affecting results

Limited generalization evaluation: primarily natural image classification; noticeably worse performance on ObjectNet/COCO than DINOv2; no evaluation on other domains (medical, satellite, documents); noise augmentation appears dataset-dependent

Computational cost remains problematic: despite 25× speedup, still requires K=20 passes per image, resulting in 20,000+ inferences for 1000-class problems—impractical compared to single-pass discriminative models; paper acknowledges but doesn't adequately address

strengths: Clear problem identification with intuitive motivation (token order affects AR classification); well-illustrated via Figure 1
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple baseline families (discriminative, diffusion, joint, AR) and diverse benchmarks (ImageNet variants, WILDS distribution shifts)
Significant practical efficiency gains (25× speedup over diffusion classifiers) with clear accuracy-efficiency trade-offs documented
Thorough experimental details supporting reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, ablation studies on tokenizers/likelihood strategies, promised code release
Insightful analysis with effective visualizations (per-token likelihoods, accuracy heatmaps, prefix length analysis) and honest error analysis showing common failure modes
Fair comparison with controlled architecture sizes and image resolutions across baselines
Robust evaluation on distribution shifts via WILDS datasets and multiple OOD benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of Jensen's inequality to marginalize over token orders—not a novel methodological advance

Heavy reliance on single model (RandAR): nearly all experiments use RandAR with only limited RAR evaluation requiring retraining; generalization beyond RandAR's specific design (position instruction tokens) is unclear

Does not achieve overall state-of-the-art: RandAR-XL underperforms DINOv2-XL by 1.4% on ImageNet-Val and 0.112 on IN-A; claiming 'competitive' while consistently losing to strongest baseline is misleading

Computational cost concerns underaddressed: while 25× faster than diffusion, requires K=20 passes × 1000 classes = 20,000 evaluations; comparison to single-pass DINOv2 shows practical disadvantage for deployment

Noise augmentation appears crucial yet underexplored: Table 4 shows consistent improvements but treated as afterthought in Section 6.4, making it unclear whether order marginalization or augmentation drives gains
Limited theoretical understanding: why averaging random orders captures contextual information is not deeply explained; interpretation of optimal prefix length (50-80 tokens) appears post-hoc
Weak justification for using lower bound (Eq. 5) over direct likelihood: explanation that 'RandAR was trained on Equation 5' lacks depth and appears implementation-contingent rather than principled
Questionable generation-classification decoupling: Appendix H shows FID doesn't correlate with accuracy, raising fundamental question about value of generative pretraining versus supervised training

Generalization concerns: Section G shows notably weaker results on non-image-centric datasets (ObjectNet: RandAR 0.339 vs DINOv2 0.439; COCO: RandAR 0.378 vs DINOv2 0.418), suggesting optimization for centered single-object ImageNet distribution
Cherry-picked motivation: Figure 1 shows clear order sensitivity, but no quantitative analysis of how prevalent this issue is across the full dataset
Incremental contribution: paper essentially applies concurrent work (RandAR) to classification with averaging—more of a benchmark/application than methodological advance
Limited supervised baselines: ResNets in Table 10 are dated; no trained-from-scratch supervised ViT comparison at same resolution for rigorous assessment
Weakened 'state-of-the-art among GCs' claim: winning within already-less-competitive generative classification domain while remaining inferior to discriminative methods limits significance
Method section (Section 4) too brief for core contribution; important details on noise augmentation and evaluation protocols relegated to appendices

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: clearly demonstrates that token order significantly affects AR-based classification (Figure 1), motivating the need for order marginalization

Strong comprehensive experiments: outperforms diffusion classifiers across in-domain and OOD benchmarks while being 25× faster; first work comparing generative classifiers with state-of-the-art SSL methods (DINOv2)
Thorough empirical validation: extensive ablations (tokenizers, likelihood strategies, noise augmentation), multiple baseline families, diverse benchmarks (ImageNet variants, WILDS, ObjectNet, COCO)

Insightful analysis: per-token discriminative log-likelihoods and accuracy visualizations (Figs 3-5) effectively show how different orders capture different spatial information; prefix-length analysis reveals importance of intermediate tokens
Practical value: achieves competitive classification with substantial efficiency improvements; demonstrates strong robustness to distribution shifts on WILDS benchmarks
Theoretical grounding: establishes connection to masked diffusion models (Appendix D); clear mathematical formulation of order-marginalized classification framework
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily applies order marginalization (Jensen's lower bound) to an existing model (RandAR); contribution is more engineering-focused than introducing new concepts

Heavy reliance on single model: RandAR is stated as 'only publicly available' any-order AR model; Section 6.6 generalization to RAR-B requires non-standard training; limits confidence in generalizability

Overstated comparison with SSL methods: RandAR-XL trails DINOv2-XL by 1.4% on in-domain accuracy and underperforms significantly on IN-A (23.3% vs 36.3%); claims of 'competitive performance' somewhat misleading

Shallow mechanistic understanding: paper demonstrates that order matters but provides limited insight into why different orders capture different information; explanation that averaging 'captures contextual information' is intuitive but not rigorously analyzed

Weak justification for lower bound: using Jensen's inequality (Eq. 5) instead of direct MC estimate (Eq. 4) works empirically but justification ('RandAR was trained on Eq. 5') is post-hoc rationalization rather than principled

VQ-VAE tokenizer dependency: performance sensitive to tokenizer choice (Table 4); unclear if improvements transfer to other tokenization methods or represent fundamental benefits of order marginalization
Misleading efficiency claims: 'up to 25×' speedup only vs worst-case diffusion (250 steps); RandAR with K=20 still requires 20 forward passes, and realistic speedup varies significantly

Incomplete experimental comparisons: models trained from scratch differ from released DINOv2 (ImageNet-21K pretrained); WILDS experiments use small sample sizes where findings may not generalize; some model-specific tricks (e.g., SiT ϵ-prediction)
